title: GST Statutory Framework: Taxable Event, Scope of Supply & Competing Schedules

parts.title: The Taxable Event Revolution: From Manufacture/Sale to 'Supply' under Section 7
parts.say:
Welcome to Day 6 of Corporate Taxation & GST. Today, we inaugurate Block 2: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) Architecture, Supply Mechanics & Input Tax Credit Systems. Over the first five days of this curriculum, you examined the corporate tax foundations: deferred tax accounting under ASC 740 and IAS 12, Modigliani-Miller debt tax shields, OECD transfer pricing models, and direct tax depreciation timing. Now, we transition into the single largest indirect tax reform in modern commercial history: the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and Value-Added Tax (VAT) architecture.

Prior to the implementation of GST, indirect taxation was plagued by severe fragmentation and cascading 'tax-on-tax' inefficiencies. Under the pre-GST regime, the central government levied Central Excise Duty on the 'manufacture' of goods, State governments levied Value Added Tax (VAT) or Central Sales Tax (CST) on the 'sale' of goods, and the Centre levied Service Tax on the 'provision' of services. In addition, businesses were burdened by Entry Tax, Octroi, Luxury Tax, and Entertainment Tax. Crucially, credit fungibility across these silos was legally blocked: a service provider could not offset state VAT paid on capital goods against central service tax liability. This created massive cascading tax cascades, embedded cost inflation, and extensive litigation over whether complex transactions (such as software licensing, works contracts, or restaurant dining) constituted a 'sale of goods' or a 'provision of service'.

The Goods and Services Tax eradicated these archaic distinctions by replacing multiple taxable events with a single, unified constitutional trigger: 'Supply'. Under Section 7(1)(a) of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, supply encompasses all forms of supply of goods or services or both, such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, license, rental, lease, or disposal made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business. To constitute a taxable supply under Section 7(1)(a), four foundational pillars must simultaneously converge: (1) there must be goods or services; (2) the transfer must take one of the recognized supply forms; (3) there must be quid pro quo consideration (monetary or non-monetary); and (4) the transaction must occur in the course or furtherance of commercial business.

In this opening part, we construct an enterprise Supply Classification & Taxable Event Engine in Python. We programmatically validate transactions against the statutory criteria of Section 7(1)(a), distinguish between commercial activities and personal non-business transfers, model the elimination of cascading tax burdens, and compute the effective tax savings realized by transitioning from legacy cascading regimes to unified GST supply frameworks.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from typing import Dict, List, Optional

@dataclass
class CommercialTransaction:
    tx_id: str
    description: str
    is_goods_or_services: bool
    supply_form: str         # 'sale', 'transfer', 'barter', 'license', 'lease', 'disposal'
    has_consideration: bool
    consideration_amount: float
    in_course_of_business: bool
    legacy_excise_rate: float
    legacy_vat_rate: float
    gst_rate: float

class SupplyValidationEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_section7_1a(tx: CommercialTransaction) -> Dict:
        # Test the 4 statutory conditions of Section 7(1)(a)
        cond1 = tx.is_goods_or_services
        cond2 = tx.supply_form.lower() in ['sale', 'transfer', 'barter', 'exchange', 'license', 'rental', 'lease', 'disposal']
        cond3 = tx.has_consideration and tx.consideration_amount > 0.0
        cond4 = tx.in_course_of_business
        
        is_taxable_supply = cond1 and cond2 and cond3 and cond4
        
        # Cascade modeling: Legacy vs GST
        # In legacy, VAT was charged on (Base + Excise Duty)
        excise_duty = tx.consideration_amount * tx.legacy_excise_rate
        legacy_vat_base = tx.consideration_amount + excise_duty
        legacy_vat = legacy_vat_base * tx.legacy_vat_rate
        total_legacy_tax = excise_duty + legacy_vat
        cascading_tax_on_tax = excise_duty * tx.legacy_vat_rate
        
        # GST unified tax (No tax-on-tax)
        gst_tax = tx.consideration_amount * tx.gst_rate if is_taxable_supply else 0.0
        effective_tax_saving = total_legacy_tax - gst_tax
        
        return {
            'tx_id': tx.tx_id,
            'description': tx.description,
            'is_taxable_supply_sec7': is_taxable_supply,
            'consideration_base': tx.consideration_amount,
            'legacy_total_tax': round(total_legacy_tax, 2),
            'legacy_cascading_component': round(cascading_tax_on_tax, 2),
            'gst_total_tax': round(gst_tax, 2),
            'net_tax_saving_under_gst': round(effective_tax_saving, 2)
        }

tx_commercial = CommercialTransaction(
    tx_id='TX-801', description='Industrial Valve Supply to Refinery',
    is_goods_or_services=True, supply_form='sale', has_consideration=True,
    consideration_amount=100000.0, in_course_of_business=True,
    legacy_excise_rate=0.125, legacy_vat_rate=0.145, gst_rate=0.18
)
engine = SupplyValidationEngine()
res = engine.evaluate_section7_1a(tx_commercial)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
parts.codeNotes: Validates the 4 statutory pillars of Section 7(1)(a) CGST Act, demonstrating how cascading tax-on-tax (Excise compounding into VAT base) is eliminated under GST.
parts.example: Under pre-GST law, a manufacturer selling industrial equipment for $100,000 paid 12.5% Central Excise ($12,500). State VAT of 14.5% was then charged on $112,500, creating $16,312.50 of VAT. Total tax was $28,812.50, containing $1,812.50 of pure cascading tax-on-tax. Under GST at 18%, tax is exactly $18,000, saving the customer $10,812.50.
parts.tryIt: Modify the code to model a personal car sale by an individual employee (in_course_of_business=False) and verify that Section 7(1)(a) returns is_taxable_supply=False.

check.question: Under Section 7(1)(a) of the CGST Act, which of the following is an absolute prerequisite for an activity to constitute a standard taxable supply?
options: The activity must be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business.
The transaction must involve an export of goods outside the territorial waters of the country.
The payment must be received exclusively through sovereign central bank digital currency.
The transaction must be certified by an independent statutory chartered accountant before invoice generation.
check.why: Section 7(1)(a) mandates that the supply must be for a consideration and in the course or furtherance of business. Transactions lacking consideration fall outside Section 7(1)(a) unless specifically captured under Schedule I.

parts.title: Deemed Supplies without Consideration: Schedule I Mechanics & Related-Party Transactions
parts.say:
While consideration is a mandatory cornerstone under Section 7(1)(a), the legislature recognized that multinational corporations and conglomerates could easily circumvent tax liabilities by transferring valuable goods, intellectual property, or services between sister subsidiaries or distinct branches without charging monetary fees. To plug this evasion vulnerability, Section 7(1)(c) read with Schedule I of the CGST Act establishes 'Deemed Supplies'—activities treated as taxable supplies even when made without consideration.

Schedule I enumerates four specific, strictly construed categories of deemed supply: (1) Permanent transfer or disposal of business assets where Input Tax Credit (ITC) has been availed on such assets; (2) Supply of goods or services between 'distinct persons' (e.g., branches of the same corporate legal entity located in different states with separate GSTINs) or between 'related persons' when made in the course or furtherance of business, with a statutory carve-out for employee gifts up to INR 50,000 per financial year; (3) Supply of goods between a principal and an agent; and (4) Import of services by a taxable person from a related person or from any of his other establishments outside India, in the course or furtherance of business.

The concept of 'Distinct Persons' under Section 25(4) and 25(5) is critical for multi-state enterprises. In GST jurisprudence, each state registration represents a distinct legal taxable entity. Consequently, when an IT company transfers high-end laptops or servers from its Bengaluru headquarters to its Mumbai branch office without invoicing any consideration, this internal corporate movement constitutes a deemed taxable supply under Entry 2 of Schedule I. GST must be calculated and paid via IGST, which the recipient Mumbai branch can simultaneously claim as Input Tax Credit (ITC), provided credit restrictions do not apply.

In this second part, we develop a Schedule I Deemed Supply Compliance Engine in Python. We programmatically evaluate inter-branch stock transfers, test whether ITC was originally availed on disposed corporate assets, track the annual gift exemption threshold for corporate employees, and compute the deemed taxable value and GST liability.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, List

@dataclass
class DeemedSupplyCandidate:
    candidate_id: str
    nature: str             # 'ASSET_DISPOSAL', 'BRANCH_TRANSFER', 'EMPLOYEE_GIFT', 'IMPORT_SERVICE'
    market_value: float
    itc_availed_originally: bool
    is_distinct_or_related: bool
    cumulative_employee_gifts_ytd: float
    gst_rate: float

class ScheduleIEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_schedule_i(c: DeemedSupplyCandidate) -> Dict:
        is_deemed_supply = False
        taxable_value = 0.0
        rationale = ''
        
        if c.nature == 'ASSET_DISPOSAL':
            # Entry 1: Permanent transfer where ITC was availed
            if c.itc_availed_originally:
                is_deemed_supply = True
                taxable_value = c.market_value
                rationale = 'Entry 1: Permanent disposal of business asset on which ITC was claimed.'
            else:
                rationale = 'Excluded: No ITC was originally claimed on asset.'
                
        elif c.nature == 'BRANCH_TRANSFER':
            # Entry 2: Distinct persons transfer in course of business
            if c.is_distinct_or_related:
                is_deemed_supply = True
                taxable_value = c.market_value
                rationale = 'Entry 2: Supply between distinct business establishments (Sec 25(4)).'
                
        elif c.nature == 'EMPLOYEE_GIFT':
            # Proviso to Entry 2: Gifts up to 50,000 INR per year exempt
            GIFT_EXEMPTION_LIMIT = 50000.0
            total_gifts = c.cumulative_employee_gifts_ytd + c.market_value
            if total_gifts > GIFT_EXEMPTION_LIMIT:
                is_deemed_supply = True
                taxable_value = total_gifts  # Once breached, entire value becomes taxable
                rationale = f'Entry 2 Proviso: Employee gifts ({total_gifts}) exceed exemption cap of 50,000.'
            else:
                rationale = f'Exempt: Total gifts ({total_gifts}) within 50,000 statutory cap.'
                
        gst_payable = taxable_value * c.gst_rate if is_deemed_supply else 0.0
        
        return {
            'candidate_id': c.candidate_id,
            'nature': c.nature,
            'is_deemed_supply_schedule_i': is_deemed_supply,
            'taxable_value': round(taxable_value, 2),
            'gst_rate': c.gst_rate,
            'gst_payable': round(gst_payable, 2),
            'legal_rationale': rationale
        }

transfer = DeemedSupplyCandidate(
    candidate_id='SCH1-01', nature='BRANCH_TRANSFER', market_value=250000.0,
    itc_availed_originally=True, is_distinct_or_related=True,
    cumulative_employee_gifts_ytd=0.0, gst_rate=0.18
)
res = ScheduleIEngine.evaluate_schedule_i(transfer)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
parts.codeNotes: Implements statutory logic for Schedule I deemed supplies without consideration, enforcing Section 25 distinct-person branch transfers and the INR 50,000 employee gift proviso.
parts.example: An enterprise donates 50 obsolete laptops (open market value $25,000) to a local charity. Because the company originally claimed $4,500 of ITC when purchasing those laptops, Entry 1 of Schedule I triggers a deemed supply: the company must self-assess and pay $4,500 in GST despite receiving zero cash consideration.
parts.tryIt: Test an EMPLOYEE_GIFT candidate with cumulative_employee_gifts_ytd=35000 and current market_value=20000. Verify that exceeding the 50,000 cap triggers Schedule I tax liability.

check.question: Under Schedule I of the CGST Act, which of the following transactions without consideration is classified as a deemed taxable supply?
options: Transfer of goods between distinct establishments (branches) of the same company having separate GSTINs.
Personal household services rendered by a mother to her children without payment.
Gifts given by an employer to an employee worth a total of INR 25,000 during a financial year.
Disposal of personal residential furniture where no input tax credit was ever claimed.
check.why: Entry 2 of Schedule I specifically designates supplies between distinct persons (different branch registrations of the same enterprise under Section 25) as deemed supplies even when made without consideration.

parts.title: Categorization Matrix: Schedule II Classification as 'Goods' vs 'Services'
parts.say:
Once an activity satisfies the criteria of being a supply under Section 7, the tax administrator faces a vital classification dilemma: Is the transaction a supply of 'Goods' or a supply of 'Services'? This determination is profoundly significant because it dictates the applicable tax rate, the Time of Supply rules under Section 12 versus Section 13, the Place of Supply rules, and the documentation requirements (e.g., e-way bill generation mandates for goods).

To resolve chronic historic litigation surrounding complex contracts, Section 7(1)(aa) read with Schedule II of the CGST Act establishes explicit statutory classification rules. Schedule II acts as a definitive categorizing engine for ambiguous activities: (1) Transfer of title in goods is a supply of goods, but transfer of right to use goods without transfer of title is explicitly a supply of services; (2) Any lease, tenancy, easement, or license to occupy land or commercial buildings is a supply of services; (3) Any treatment or process applied to another person's goods (job work) is a supply of services; (4) Development, design, programming, customization, or adaptation of information technology software is statutorily classified as a supply of services; (5) Agreeing to the obligation to refrain from an act, or to tolerate an act (non-compete fees and liquidated damages), is a supply of services; and (6) Composite supplies like Works Contracts (construction of immovable property) and Restaurant/Catering services are permanently classified as supplies of services.

The classification of software and intellectual property under Schedule II brought immense clarity to enterprise commerce. Under pre-GST law, software sold in a shrink-wrapped CD was taxed as goods under State VAT, while customized code was taxed as services under Service Tax, leading to double-taxation disputes. Schedule II Paragraph 5(d) conclusively declared the development and adaptation of software to be a service, harmonizing the entire digital economy under single-point service taxation.

In this third part, we program an enterprise Schedule II Classification Engine in Python. We map transaction parameters to statutory Schedule II paragraphs, determine whether an activity is legally goods or services, assign the correct statutory provisions, and route the transaction to the appropriate Time of Supply governance workflow.

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict

@dataclass
class CommercialActivity:
    activity_id: str
    title: str
    transfers_title: bool
    is_land_or_building_lease: bool
    is_job_work_on_others_goods: bool
    is_software_customization: bool
    is_works_contract_immovable: bool
    is_restaurant_catering: bool

class ScheduleIIClassifier:
    @staticmethod
    def classify(act: CommercialActivity) -> Dict:
        classification = 'UNKNOWN'
        paragraph_ref = ''
        tos_section = ''
        
        if act.transfers_title:
            classification = 'SUPPLY_OF_GOODS'
            paragraph_ref = 'Schedule II, Para 1(a): Transfer of title in goods.'
            tos_section = 'Section 12 (Time of Supply for Goods)'
        elif act.is_software_customization:
            classification = 'SUPPLY_OF_SERVICES'
            paragraph_ref = 'Schedule II, Para 5(d): IT Software development/adaptation.'
            tos_section = 'Section 13 (Time of Supply for Services)'
        elif act.is_works_contract_immovable:
            classification = 'SUPPLY_OF_SERVICES'
            paragraph_ref = 'Schedule II, Para 6(a): Works contract for immovable property.'
            tos_section = 'Section 13 (Time of Supply for Services)'
        elif act.is_land_or_building_lease:
            classification = 'SUPPLY_OF_SERVICES'
            paragraph_ref = 'Schedule II, Para 2(b): Lease or letting out of commercial building.'
            tos_section = 'Section 13 (Time of Supply for Services)'
        elif act.is_job_work_on_others_goods:
            classification = 'SUPPLY_OF_SERVICES'
            paragraph_ref = 'Schedule II, Para 3: Treatment/process applied to another person\'s goods.'
            tos_section = 'Section 13 (Time of Supply for Services)'
        elif act.is_restaurant_catering:
            classification = 'SUPPLY_OF_SERVICES'
            paragraph_ref = 'Schedule II, Para 6(b): Supply of food/drink for human consumption.'
            tos_section = 'Section 13 (Time of Supply for Services)'
        else:
            classification = 'SUPPLY_OF_SERVICES'
            paragraph_ref = 'Schedule II, Para 1(b): Transfer of right in goods without transfer of title.'
            tos_section = 'Section 13 (Time of Supply for Services)'
            
        return {
            'activity_id': act.activity_id,
            'title': act.title,
            'statutory_classification': classification,
            'schedule_ii_provision': paragraph_ref,
            'governing_time_of_supply_rule': tos_section
        }

erp_project = CommercialActivity(
    activity_id='ACT-901', title='Enterprise Cloud ERP Customization & Implementation',
    transfers_title=False, is_land_or_building_lease=False,
    is_job_work_on_others_goods=False, is_software_customization=True,
    is_works_contract_immovable=False, is_restaurant_catering=False
)
res = ScheduleIIClassifier.classify(erp_project)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
parts.codeNotes: Categorizes commercial activities into Goods versus Services under Schedule II CGST Act, assigning governing Time of Supply statutory sections.
parts.example: A construction contractor builds a corporate office tower. The contract includes steel, cement, architectural labor, and engineering supervision. Under Schedule II Para 6(a), this entire composite bundle is conclusively deemed a 'Supply of Services' (Works Contract), preventing split tax assessments across goods and labor.
parts.tryIt: Modify the code to test an equipment lease where the title remains with the lessor (transfers_title=False) and verify that it classifies as a Supply of Services under Para 1(b).

check.question: Under Schedule II of the CGST Act, how is the development, design, programming, and customization of information technology software categorized?
options: Conclusively as a Supply of Services.
Conclusively as a Supply of Goods.
As an exempt non-taxable supply under Schedule III.
As a dual composite supply taxed under both Goods and Services schedules independently.
check.why: Schedule II Paragraph 5(d) explicitly classifies the development, design, programming, customization, adaptation, upgradation, enhancement, and implementation of IT software as a Supply of Services.

parts.title: Composite vs Mixed Supplies: Section 8 Bundling Rules & Principal Supply Invariants
parts.say:
In modern commercial practice, businesses rarely sell individual products in clinical isolation; instead, they bundle goods and services together to create compelling consumer value propositions. For example, a laptop is sold bundled with a 3-year warranty and a carrying bag; a flight ticket includes an in-flight meal and baggage handling; or a holiday festival gift box contains chocolates, dry fruits, canned juice, and a branded ceramic mug. If the bundled elements attract divergent GST tax rates (e.g., chocolates at 18%, dry fruits at 12%, ceramic mugs at 28%), how must the overall invoice be taxed?

Section 8 of the CGST Act establishes the legal architecture to resolve bundled transactions by dividing them into two distinct statutory categories: Composite Supplies and Mixed Supplies. Under Section 2(30), a 'Composite Supply' consists of two or more taxable supplies of goods or services or both, which are naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction with each other in the ordinary course of business, one of which is a 'Principal Supply'. Under Section 8(a), a composite supply is taxed entirely at the GST rate applicable to the Principal Supply. For instance, when purchasing an expensive machine with mandatory transit insurance and installation, the machinery is the principal supply; the insurance and transport elements take on the tax rate of the machine, regardless of their standalone rates.

Conversely, under Section 2(74), a 'Mixed Supply' consists of two or more individual supplies of goods or services, or any combination thereof, made in conjunction with each other by a taxable person for a single price, which do NOT constitute a composite supply (i.e., they are artificially bundled and could easily be sold separately). Under Section 8(b), the statutory consequence of a mixed supply is intentionally punitive: the entire bundle is taxed at the highest rate of tax applicable to any single item contained within the package! If a gift basket sold for $100 contains dry fruits (12%), chocolates (18%), and a cosmetic fragrance (28%), the entire $100 invoice is taxed at 28%.

In this fourth part, we engineer an enterprise Section 8 Bundling & Tax Optimization Engine in Python. We inspect product bundles, test for natural commercial bundling versus artificial combination, identify the principal supply based on economic dominance, and compute the tax liability under both composite and mixed supply rules to guide corporate packaging and pricing strategies.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, List

@dataclass
class BundleItem:
    name: str
    standalone_price: float
    gst_rate: float
    is_primary_intent: bool

@dataclass
class BundledPackage:
    package_id: str
    package_title: str
    single_invoice_price: float
    is_naturally_bundled_in_trade: bool
    items: List[BundleItem]

class Section8BundlingEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_bundle(pkg: BundledPackage) -> Dict:
        if pkg.is_naturally_bundled_in_trade:
            # Section 8(a): Composite Supply -> Taxed at Principal Supply rate
            principal_item = next((item for item in pkg.items if item.is_primary_intent), pkg.items[0])
            effective_rate = principal_item.gst_rate
            bundle_type = 'COMPOSITE_SUPPLY (Sec 8(a))'
            rationale = f'Naturally bundled. Taxed at principal supply ({principal_item.name}) rate of {int(effective_rate*100)}%.'
        else:
            # Section 8(b): Mixed Supply -> Taxed at HIGHEST rate among items
            highest_item = max(pkg.items, key=lambda x: x.gst_rate)
            effective_rate = highest_item.gst_rate
            bundle_type = 'MIXED_SUPPLY (Sec 8(b))'
            rationale = f'Artificially bundled for single price. Taxed at highest rate ({highest_item.name}) of {int(effective_rate*100)}%.'
            
        tax_amount = pkg.single_invoice_price * effective_rate
        total_invoice_with_tax = pkg.single_invoice_price + tax_amount
        
        # Calculate what tax would be if unbundled/sold separately
        unbundled_tax = sum(item.standalone_price * item.gst_rate for item in pkg.items)
        packaging_tax_variance = tax_amount - unbundled_tax
        
        return {
            'package_id': pkg.package_id,
            'title': pkg.package_title,
            'bundle_classification': bundle_type,
            'effective_gst_rate': effective_rate,
            'single_price': pkg.single_invoice_price,
            'gst_tax_payable': round(tax_amount, 2),
            'total_invoice': round(total_invoice_with_tax, 2),
            'unbundled_tax_comparison': round(unbundled_tax, 2),
            'packaging_tax_penalty': round(packaging_tax_variance, 2),
            'legal_analysis': rationale
        }

# Example 1: Executive Festive Hamper (Mixed Supply)
hamper_items = [
    BundleItem('Imported Belgian Chocolates', 3000.0, 0.18, False),
    BundleItem('Roasted Almonds & Pistachios', 2000.0, 0.12, False),
    BundleItem('Designer Crystal Decanter', 5000.0, 0.28, False)
]
festive_hamper = BundledPackage('PKG-701', 'Diwali Corporate Gift Hamper', 10000.0, False, hamper_items)
res = Section8BundlingEngine.evaluate_bundle(festive_hamper)
print(json.dumps(res, indent=2))
parts.codeNotes: Simulates Section 8 CGST Act rules for Composite versus Mixed supplies, demonstrating the tax penalty triggered when artificially bundling items under a single price.
parts.example: A mobile phone ($800, 18% GST) is sold with a fast charger in the box. Because smartphones and chargers are naturally bundled in the ordinary course of trade, this is a Composite Supply taxed at 18%. But if a retailer sells a gift box containing a phone (18%), a dry fruit tin (12%), and luxury perfume (28%) for a single price of $1,000, Section 8(b) taxes the entire $1,000 at 28%.
parts.tryIt: Change is_naturally_bundled_in_trade to True and set is_primary_intent=True for Belgian Chocolates (0.18). Observe how Section 8(a) treats it as a Composite Supply taxed at 18%.

check.question: Under Section 8(b) of the CGST Act, how is a Mixed Supply consisting of goods attracting divergent rates of 5%, 12%, and 28% supplied for a single price taxed?
options: The entire supply is taxed at the highest rate of 28%.
The supply is taxed at the weighted mathematical average rate of the items.
Each item is taxed separately by demanding a post-hoc breakdown of the single price.
The entire bundle is deemed non-taxable because individual consideration is not segregated.
check.why: Section 8(b) mandates that a mixed supply comprising two or more supplies shall be treated as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the highest rate of tax.

parts.title: Non-Supplies & Statutory Carve-Outs: Schedule III Negative List Governance
parts.say:
In any comprehensive tax system, defining what lies outside the tax net is just as critical as defining taxable scope. If the statutory boundary of 'Supply' remained unbounded, essential civic, employment, and constitutional functions could be subjected to unwarranted taxation disputes. To provide absolute certainty and safeguard core socio-economic relationships, Section 7(2)(a) read with Schedule III of the CGST Act establishes the statutory 'Negative List'—activities or transactions which shall be treated neither as a supply of goods nor as a supply of services.

Schedule III contains eight vital statutory carve-outs: (1) Services by an employee to the employer in the course of or in relation to his employment (salary and wages are completely immune from GST); (2) Services by any court or tribunal established under any law; (3) Functions performed by Members of Parliament, State Legislators, Municipal Councillors, and constitutional officeholders (such as the President, Governors, or Judges); (4) Services of funeral, burial, crematorium, or mortuary, including transportation of the deceased; (5) Sale of land and, subject to Schedule II Para 5(b), sale of completed commercial or residential buildings where the entire consideration is received after issuance of the completion certificate; (6) Actionable claims, other than specified betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, or online money gaming; (7) Out-and-out merchant trade transactions (supply of goods from a place in the non-taxable territory to another place in the non-taxable territory without such goods entering India); and (8) Supply of warehoused goods to any person before clearance for home consumption.

The employment exemption in Schedule III Entry 1 has profound corporate ramifications. While regular employee salaries, statutory bonuses, and contractual employment benefits are exempt from GST, payments made to independent contractors, retainers, freelance consultants, or sitting fees paid to non-executive directors fall outside Schedule III. Sitting fees paid to company directors are subject to GST under the Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM), requiring the company to pay tax directly to the government treasury.

In this fifth part, we build an enterprise Schedule III Negative List Gating Engine in Python. We screen corporate disbursements, distinguish between employment contracts and independent service retainers, verify real estate completion certificates to validate land/building tax immunity, and generate an executive GST Negative List Audit Certificate.
parts.code:
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, List

@dataclass
class CorporateDisbursement:
    disbursement_id: str
    payee: str
    category: str           # 'EMPLOYEE_SALARY', 'DIRECTOR_SITTING_FEE', 'SALE_COMPLETED_BUILDING', 'MERCHANT_TRADE'
    amount: float
    has_employment_contract: bool
    has_completion_cert_before_sale: bool
    goods_entered_domestic_territory: bool

class ScheduleIIIEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_negative_list(d: CorporateDisbursement) -> Dict:
        is_schedule_iii_negative_list = False
        gst_taxable = False
        applicable_mechanism = 'NONE'
        entry_ref = ''
        
        if d.category == 'EMPLOYEE_SALARY':
            if d.has_employment_contract:
                is_schedule_iii_negative_list = True
                gst_taxable = False
                entry_ref = 'Schedule III, Entry 1: Services by employee to employer in course of employment.'
            else:
                is_schedule_iii_negative_list = False
                gst_taxable = True
                applicable_mechanism = 'FORWARD_CHARGE (Independent Contractor)'
                
        elif d.category == 'DIRECTOR_SITTING_FEE':
            # Not an employee service in course of employment
            is_schedule_iii_negative_list = False
            gst_taxable = True
            applicable_mechanism = 'REVERSE_CHARGE_MECHANISM (RCM - Company Pays)'
            entry_ref = 'Excluded from Sch III. Subject to RCM under Sec 9(3).'
            
        elif d.category == 'SALE_COMPLETED_BUILDING':
            if d.has_completion_cert_before_sale:
                is_schedule_iii_negative_list = True
                gst_taxable = False
                entry_ref = 'Schedule III, Entry 5: Sale of completed building post-occupancy certificate.'
            else:
                is_schedule_iii_negative_list = False
                gst_taxable = True
                applicable_mechanism = 'FORWARD_CHARGE (Under-construction Real Estate)'
                
        elif d.category == 'MERCHANT_TRADE':
            if not d.goods_entered_domestic_territory:
                is_schedule_iii_negative_list = True
                gst_taxable = False
                entry_ref = 'Schedule III, Entry 7: Merchant trade from non-taxable territory to another.'
            else:
                is_schedule_iii_negative_list = False
                gst_taxable = True
                
        return {
            'disbursement_id': d.disbursement_id,
            'payee': d.payee,
            'amount': d.amount,
            'is_negative_list_schedule_iii': is_schedule_iii_negative_list,
            'gst_taxable': gst_taxable,
            'tax_mechanism': applicable_mechanism,
            'statutory_authority': entry_ref
        }

check.question: Under Schedule III of the CGST Act, which of the following activities is statutorily treated as NEITHER a supply of goods NOR a supply of services?
options: Services by an employee to the employer in the course of or in relation to his employment.
Services by an independent software architecture consultant billed under an annual master service agreement.
Director sitting fees paid to non-executive independent directors for attending board committee meetings.
Under-construction residential apartment sales where consideration was received prior to the completion certificate.
check.why: Schedule III Entry 1 explicitly excludes services rendered by an employee to their employer in the course of or in relation to their employment from the definition of supply.
